title: Hávamál
source: Gustav Neckel, Edda: Die Lieder des Codex Regius nebst verwandten Denkmälern, 1st edition (Heidelberg: Carl Winter, 1914), Hávamál, stanzas 138–164, pp. 39–43. Text transcribed from Neckel's page images and reproduced in his normalization exactly — þ, ð, æ, œ, the nasal vowel ǫ, ø, acute length-marks, the -z/-az/-oz middle endings, i for j (siálfr, þióða, fiǫturr, Lióð), -om datives, þvíat as one word. Italicized (editorially emended or expanded) letters are set as plain letters; the emendations that change the sense are noted — among them 150,3 fólk, where the Codex Regius reads the dative fólki. Neckel's rows of spaced dots marking the lacunae after 145,5 and after 146,3 are kept, dot for dot and row for row, and mirrored in the literal layer. In his apparatus, bold sigla are manuscripts (R = Codex Regius, the only witness for these stanzas) and italic sigla are scholars or their editions (B = Bugge, C = Corpus poeticum boreale, G = Gering, Gv = Grundtvig, H = Hildebrand, J = Finnur Jónsson, K = the Copenhagen edition of 1787–1828, L = Lüning, M = Munch, Mh = Müllenhoff, Mk = Mogk, R = Rask, S = Sijmons); the notes here follow that distinction, and say so at 149,3, where both the bold R (Codex Regius) and the italic R (Rask) stand in the same entry, and at the places where the italic H is Hildebrand and not the Hauksbók. Neckel's typeface makes capital Þ look like capital D; every initial-D word here was checked against Cleasby–Vigfússon, and the three that survive as true D (Dáinn, Dvalinn, Dellings) stand beside a genuine thorn in st. 160 for comparison. Eddic poems are cited by stanza, so the margin numbers are stanza numbers. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed classical Old Icelandic, c. 1200. Translations made fresh from the original.
about: The end of the Hávamál, and the strangest thing in it. After the counsels to Loddfáfnir the poem changes speaker and subject entirely: a voice says that he hung on a windy tree nine whole nights, wounded with a spear and given to Óðinn — himself to his own self — on a tree of which no one knows from what roots it runs. No one gave him bread or drink; he looked down, took up runes, took them screaming, and fell back from there. That is the Rúnatal, stanzas 138–145: the runes' origin, the carvers who cut them for each kind of being (Óðinn for the Æsir, Dáinn for the elves, Dvalinn for the dwarfs, Ásviðr for the giants), and a series of questions — do you know how one shall carve, how read, how stain, how ask, how sacrifice? — that break off into a row of dots where the manuscript's text runs out. From 146 the poem becomes the Ljóðatal, the tally of charms: eighteen of them, counted off one by one, each in the same formula, That I know as the … The charms are for blunting an enemy's edges, for loosening fetters, for stopping a shaft in flight, for turning a wound back on the man who worked it, for quieting a storm at sea, for putting hag-riders to flight home out of their skins, for speaking with a hanged man, for a woman's love and for keeping it. The eighteenth he will tell to no one but a sister or the woman in his arms. Then the poem closes: now the sayings of the High One are chanted in the High One's hall, of great use to the sons of men, of no use to the sons of giants — hail to him who chanted, hail to him who knows, may he profit who took it in, hail to those who listened. Everything printed here is a modern editor's normalization of a single manuscript, the Codex Regius (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270); the verse is ljóðaháttr, and the margin numbers are stanza numbers.

sentences.t:
Veit ek, at ek hekk
vindga meiði á
nætr allar nío,
geiri undaðr
ok gefinn Óðni,
siálfr siálfom mér,
á þeim meiði,
er manngi veit,
hvers hann af rótom renn.
sentences.l:
I know that I hung
on a windy tree
all nine nights,
wounded with a spear
and given to Óðinn,
I myself to my own self,
on that tree
of which no man knows
from whose roots it runs.
sentences.i: I know that I hung on a windy tree all nine nights, wounded with a spear and given to Óðinn — I myself to my own self — on that tree of which no man knows from whose roots it runs.
sentences.n: The most famous stanza in the poem, and the first thing to say about it is that nothing in it is explained. The hanging, the wound, the nine nights and the gift are stated and left; the poem never says who hung him, what the tree is, or what the giving accomplished. We translate the plain words and add nothing. Two grammatical points carry most of the weight. geiri undaðr is a bare dative of instrument with a past participle — 'wounded with a spear', with no agent named, and the literal layer keeps the agent unnamed. siálfr siálfom mér is nominative beside dative: siálfr agrees with the ek that hung, siálfom mér is the dative governed by gefinn, so the giver and the one given to are the same person twice over. Old Norse can set the two cases side by side; English has to spell out 'I myself to my own self' and even then loses the rhyme of the forms. The last two lines are a relative clause of the loosest kind: er is the indeclinable particle, and hvers is a genitive dependent on rótom, 'from the roots of what'. hvers is genitive singular and rótom dative plural feminine, so the two cannot agree — hvers depends on rótom rather than qualifying it, which is why the literal layer reads 'from whose roots'. renn is renna 'to run', used of a plant's springing from its root — the tree's origin is what no one knows, not its species. Neckel's apparatus records that siálfr in line 6 was added above the line in the Codex Regius, and that the Corpus poeticum boreale and Finnur Jónsson read line 2 as a compound: Vingameiði (C, capitalised as a name) or vingameiði (J, lowercase). On the first the tree is called something rather than described; on the second it is an appellative compound, not a name. Two structural things worth knowing here, since both parts now sit side by side in the reader. First, Neckel's apparatus to st. 111 records that Heusler took that stanza — the one that opens the Loddfáfnir counsels, 'It is time to chant, on the sage's seat … of runes I heard them speak' — as the introduction to 138 ff. rather than to what follows it; on Heusler's reading the Rúnatal begins there, one part earlier. Second, this is the first of the two movements shipped together here: 138–145 tell what happened on the tree, and from 146 the poem turns into a numbered list of charms.

sentences.t:
Við hleifi mik seldo
né við hornigi;
nýsta ek niðr:
nam ek upp rúnar,
œpandi nam:
fell ek aptr þaðan.
sentences.l:
For a loaf they did not hand me over,
nor for any horn;
I peered down:
I took up runes,
crying out I took them:
I fell back from there.
sentences.i: For a loaf they did not hand me over, nor for any horn. I peered down; I took up runes, took them crying out, and fell back from there.
sentences.n: Line 1 will not construe comfortably as Neckel prints it, and the honest thing is to say so. seldo is selia 'to hand over, to give in exchange', and mik is accusative — the object of the verb, not a recipient. So the Norse says, word for word, that for a loaf they did not hand HIM over, and við + dat. after selia is the ordinary construction of price or exchange (selia við verði 'to sell for a price'). That is the difficulty: nothing in the situation is bought or sold. Whatever verb is read, the thing done is done to him, and what the stanza says on any reading is that the hanging was a fast — no food, no drink, nine nights. The negation is a separate matter and the note has to be exact about it. It is carried by ne in line 2, a negative conjunction that in Eddic verse can negate on its own, reinforced by the suffixed -gi on hornigi (the same suffix as in manngi 'no man' and vættki 'nothing'); the negation has to reach back over line 1, which is why our literal layer supplies 'not' there. What the editors attack is the verb, not the negation: Bugge reads sœldo 'refreshed' (to svalr), Eiríkr Magnússon sældo 'gladdened' (to sæll), Sijmons sǫddo 'sated' (to seðia). All three still depend on ne/-gi to negate; they fix the verb's sense, not the sentence's negative. Neckel keeps the manuscript's seldo and leaves the difficulty standing, and so do we. nýsa is 'to peer, to pry, to look searchingly', and niðr here is the adverb 'down', not the noun niðr 'kinsman' that the shared glossary carried from the Gestaþáttr. The object of the second nam is left out — 'crying out I took' — and English needs 'them'. Neckel prints þaðan with an editorial ð; the Codex Regius reads þatan. The fall is the counterpart of the rising in st. 145,9.

sentences.t:
Fimbullióð nío
nam ek af inom frægia syni
Bǫlþors, Bestlo fǫður,
ok ek drykk of gat
ins dýra miaðar,
ausinn Óðrøri.
sentences.l:
Nine mighty songs
I learned from the famous son
of Bǫlþorr, Bestla's father,
and I got a drink
of the precious mead,
besprinkled with Óðrerir.
sentences.i: Nine mighty songs I learned from the famous son of Bǫlþorr, Bestla's father, and I got a draught of the precious mead, sprinkled with Óðrerir.
sentences.n: The stanza itself says only that Bǫlþorr is Bestla's father, and that the speaker learned nine songs from Bǫlþorr's famous son. That Bestla is Óðinn's mother, and Bǫlþorr a giant — which would make the unnamed son Óðinn's uncle on his mother's side — comes from Snorri's Edda, which Neckel's apparatus gestures at with 'vgl. SnE' when it records that most editors print Bǫlþorns; the Codex Regius and Munch have Bǫlþórs. The poem never names the son. fǫður is the genitive of faðir in apposition to Bǫlþors; the manuscript first wrote syni here, on the model of line 2. nema af e-m is the ordinary idiom 'to learn from someone', so nam here is not the nema upp 'take up' of the stanza before, though the poem plainly wants them heard together. The last line is grammatically ambiguous and we have chosen: ausinn is a nominative masculine participle agreeing with the ek who got the drink, and Óðrøri is a dative — either of the thing he was sprinkled WITH ('besprinkled with Óðrerir') or of the source he was ladled OUT OF, which suits the vessel-sense of the name. The dative permits both and nothing in the grammar decides between them: ausinn agrees with ek on either reading. We have taken the dative as instrumental. Óðrerir is the mead of poetry, or the vessel holding it — the sources differ, and st. 107 has already used the name. Neckel prints the slashed ø where the Codex Regius has Óðreri and Munch Óðrœri.

sentences.t:
Þá nam ek frævaz
ok fróðr vera
ok vaxa ok vel hafaz;
orð mér af orði
orz leitaði,
verk mér af verki
verks leitaði.
sentences.l:
Then I began to thrive
and to be wise
and to grow and to fare well;
a word for me from a word
sought out a word,
a deed for me from a deed
sought out a deed.
sentences.i: Then I began to thrive, and to grow wise, and to grow and fare well: one word led me on from word to word, one deed from deed to deed.
sentences.n: nema with a following infinitive means 'to begin, to take to', not 'to take' — the same verb as st. 139's nam ek upp rúnar in a completely different construction, three lines apart. frævaz is the middle of fræva 'to bear fruit' and hafaz the middle of hafa; vel hafaz is 'to conduct oneself well, to fare well'. The last four lines are one figure stated twice, and the grammar is exact: orð is a nominative singular subject, orz a genitive object of leita (leita always takes the genitive), af orði a dative of source, and mér a dative of interest. So a word, starting from a word, sought out a word for him — and the same for deeds. It is the poem's account of how learning compounds, and it uses the same noun in three cases in two lines to say so. Finnur Jónsson deleted the second leitaði and read lines 6–7 as a single long line. Neckel's apparatus also notes that some editors assume a lacuna after this stanza, and that Mogk, following Müllenhoff, begins the 'second fragment' of the Rúnatal at 142 — the seam is real enough that the next stanza turns to address a 'you' who has not been present since the Rúnatal began.

sentences.t:
Rúnar munt þú finna
ok ráðna stafi,
miǫk stóra stafi,
miǫk stinna stafi,
er fáði fimbulþulr
ok gørðo ginnregin
ok reist hroptr rǫgna,
sentences.l:
Runes you will find
and staves read out,
very great staves,
very strong staves,
which the great sage stained
and the mighty powers made
and Hroptr of the gods carved,
sentences.i: Runes you will find, and staves read out — staves very great, staves very strong — which the great sage stained, and the mighty powers made, and Hroptr of the gods carved:
sentences.n: The address turns outward: þú appears for the first time in the part, and the stanza runs on into the next without stopping, which is why Neckel ends it with a comma. ráðna is the past participle of ráða, the verb used of reading and interpreting runes — it returns as an infinitive in the catechism of st. 144 — so the staves are ones that have been read, not merely cut. fá is likewise technical: it is 'to paint, to colour, to stain', the reddening of the carved letters, and its infinitive is one of the eight things st. 144 asks whether you know how to do. We render it 'stain' here and at 144, as at st. 80. Three clauses, three different subjects, and the same figure may stand behind two of them: fimbulþulr 'the great sage' is the word st. 80 used, and Hroptr is an Óðinn-name — so the stanza can be read as naming Óðinn twice before st. 143 names him outright. That is a reading, not a certainty; the mighty powers in between (ginnregin, the word of st. 80 again) are plural and are not him. Neckel's apparatus records that Gering rearranged lines 3–4 into a long line after 5–6 and read er reist for ok reist; that Bugge put line 6 before line 5, comparing st. 80; and that Sijmons reads ragna hróptr in line 7. Neckel prints hroptr lowercase and without the acute, and the apparatus lemma's hróptr belongs to Sijmons's reading, not to the text.

sentences.t:
Óðinn með ásom,
en fyr álfom Dáinn,
Dvalinn dvergom fyrir,
Ásviðr iǫtnom fyrir,
ek reist siálfr sumar.
sentences.l:
Óðinn among the Æsir,
but for the elves Dáinn,
Dvalinn for the dwarfs,
Ásviðr for the giants,
I myself carved some.
sentences.i: Óðinn among the Æsir; for the elves, Dáinn; Dvalinn for the dwarfs; Ásviðr for the giants — and some I carved myself.
sentences.n: The list finishes the sentence begun in st. 142: these are the carvers, one per race, with reist understood in every line but the last. sumar is an accusative plural feminine agreeing with the rúnar of st. 142,1 — 'some of them' — which is the only word in the two stanzas that reaches back across the stanza break, and it is what makes the speaker one of the carvers rather than a reporter of the list. Dáinn and Dvalinn are both dwarf-names in the catalogue in the Vǫluspá. The name Dáinn is identical in form with dáinn, the past participle of deyia, and is generally read as 'the dead one'; here Dáinn is assigned to the elves and Dvalinn to the dwarfs, and nothing explains the reassignment. Ásviðr appears nowhere else in the Codex Regius poems; the paper manuscripts read Alsviðr. Both initial D's in this stanza are genuine D's, checked letter by letter against the typeface and against Cleasby–Vigfússon — everywhere else in this part what looks like a capital D is a capital Þ. The manuscript's own arrangement is not Neckel's: the Codex Regius writes 'en fyr álfom Dvalinn Dáinn ok dvergom fyrir', with transposition marks over the two names, and Sijmons deletes the ok. Line 4 is metrically short, and Gering fills it out by supplying a fifth race — en fyr ýta sonom, 'and for the sons of men' — which would give gods, elves, dwarfs, giants and men. Neckel prints no such line and we translate what he prints. Mogk begins his 'third fragment' of the Rúnatal at the next stanza.

sentences.t:
Veitstu, hvé rísta skal?
veitstu, hvé ráða skal?
veitstu, hvé fá skal?
veitstu, hvé freista skal?
veitstu, hvé biðia skal?
veitstu, hvé blóta skal?
veitstu, hvé senda skal?
veitstu, hvé sóa skal?
sentences.l:
Do you know how one shall carve?
do you know how one shall read?
do you know how one shall stain?
do you know how one shall test?
do you know how one shall pray?
do you know how one shall sacrifice?
do you know how one shall send?
do you know how one shall slay?
sentences.i: Do you know how to carve? Do you know how to read? Do you know how to stain, and how to test? Do you know how to pray, how to sacrifice, how to send, how to slay?
sentences.n: Eight identical questions, eight infinitives, no answers. veitstu is veizt + þú fused; skal is impersonal throughout, 'one shall', with the infinitive carrying the action — the standard Old Norse way of asking whether a procedure is known. The first four verbs belong to the runes: rísta 'to cut', ráða 'to read' (the ráðna of st. 142,2), fá 'to stain' (the fáði of st. 142,5 and the verb of st. 80), freista 'to make trial of', which takes the genitive and here has no object at all. The last four belong to sacrifice: biðia 'to pray', blóta 'to offer', senda 'to send', sóa 'to slay, to make away with' — which governs the dative of its victim, and is the verb st. 109 used of what Suttungr might have done to Bǫlverkr. What senda means in a sacrificial list is not certain; dispatching the offering is the likeliest sense, and the poem does not elaborate. The stanza is a catechism and its point is the asking: everything the two preceding stanzas described as made and carved and stained is here converted into a question about the reader's competence, and st. 145 answers only the sacrificial half of it — which is why óbeðit there is rendered 'unprayed', matching biðia here. Neckel files no apparatus entry for this stanza; the remark that Mogk's 'third fragment' begins here is printed inside the entry for 143.

sentences.t:
Betra er óbeðit,
en sé ofblótit:
ey sér til gildis giǫf;
betra er ósent,
en sé ofsóit:
. . . . . . . . . . .
Svá Þundr um reist
fyr þióða rǫk;
þar hann upp um reis,
er hann aptr of kom.
sentences.l:
Better it is unprayed
than there be over-offering:
a gift ever has a requital in view;
better it is unsent
than there be over-slaying:
. . . . . . . . . . .
So Þundr carved
before the doom of peoples;
there he rose up,
when he came back.
sentences.i: Better to pray for nothing than to offer too much: a gift is always given with a return in view. Better to send nothing than to slay too much. … So Þundr carved, before the doom of the peoples; there he rose up, when he came back.
sentences.n: The answer to the last four questions of st. 144, and it is a warning against excess rather than an instruction. All four key words are impersonal neuter participles with no subject — óbeðit 'unprayed', ofblótit 'over-sacrificed', ósent 'unsent', ofsóit 'over-slaughtered' — so nobody is named as doing any of it; the literal layer keeps that shapelessness, and keeps 'unprayed' rather than 'unasked' because the verb is the biðia of 144,5. The reason stands between the two halves and is the same accounting the Gestaþáttr applies to human gifts at st. 39 and 41–42: ey sér til gildis giǫf, 'a gift ever has a requital in view'. sér here is siá 'to see', not the reflexive dative, and gildi is payment or requital — an offering creates an obligation, so an offering too large creates one too large to meet. Applying that to the gods is the stanza's real move. Neckel prints an undivided row of eleven dots after line 5, marking a line he takes to be missing. His apparatus records no damage here and files no entry for this stanza at all; the gap is an editorial judgement about the metre, not a hole in the codex. (The apparatus does note, inside the entry for st. 143, that some editors set a further lacuna after this stanza.) Then a coda in a different voice. Þundr is an Óðinn-name; um and of before the verbs are the old expletive particle, not prepositions. fyr þióða rǫk is genuinely ambiguous — rǫk is the word in ragna rǫk, and can mean the fated end of a thing or its whole course and origin, so the phrase is either 'before the doom of peoples' or 'before the beginnings of peoples', i.e. before there were nations at all. We have printed 'the doom of peoples' and the other reading stays open; English has no word that carries both ends of rǫk at once. The last two lines close the Rúnatal by answering its opening: in st. 139,6 he fell back from the tree, and here he rose up and came back. er in the last line can be 'when' or 'where'; nothing decides it. The section beginning at 146 is the Ljóðatal.

sentences.t:
Lióð ek þau kann,
er kannat þióðans kona
né mannzkis mǫgr;
. . . . .
. . . . .
. . . . .
Hiálp heitir eitt,
en þat þér hiálpa mun
við sǫkom ok sorgom
ok sútom gǫrvǫllom.
sentences.l:
Those songs I know,
which a prince's wife knows not
nor any man's son;
. . . . .
. . . . .
. . . . .
Help one is called,
and it will help you
against strifes and sorrows
and griefs one and all.
sentences.i: I know songs that no prince's wife knows, nor any man's son. … One of them is called Help, and it will help you against quarrels and sorrows and every grief there is.
sentences.n: The Ljóðatal begins, and its rule is announced in the first three lines: what he knows is what nobody else knows. kannat is kann with the suffixed negative -at, the same suffix as in bítat (st. 148) and flýgra (st. 150). þau is a neuter plural picking up lióð, held back to the end of its own line. The two people named are a high-born woman and any man at all — that is the whole social range — and the pairing sets up the eighteenth and last charm, which he will tell to no one but the woman who holds him in her arms, or his sister (st. 163). Neckel prints Gering's né in line 3; the Codex Regius reads ok, which with the negative already in kannat comes to the same sense. Grundtvig read konr 'son' for kona 'wife'. The manuscript's mannzcis has its c added above the line. Neckel then prints two rows of dots, the first divided at the caesura, so three dot-lines here — dots marking a lacuna Neckel assumes — while the editions print no gap at this point and put one after 147,3 instead; the disagreement is on the page and we keep Neckel's. This is the first charm, and the count is worth following from the start, because the poem does not number this one: st. 147 is 'the second', 148 'the third', and so on to the eighteenth at st. 163. St. 164, 'Nú ero Háva mál kveðin', closes the poem and is not a charm. So the first is identified only by being first. It is also the only one of the eighteen that is given a name — Hiálp, 'Help' — and even so the name is the whole of the description. What it is against is broad and unspecific: sǫk is a charge or a cause of strife, sorg is grief, sút is care or sickness, and gǫrvǫllom sweeps up the rest. The við of line 9 governs line 10 as well; the original does not repeat it and neither does the literal layer.

sentences.t:
Þat kann ek annat,
er þurfo ýta synir,
þeir er vilia læknar lifa.
sentences.l:
That I know as a second,
which the sons of men need,
those who want to live as healers.
sentences.i: I know a second, one that men need — those who want to live by healing.
sentences.n: The second charm, and the first to use the counting formula that will run to the end of the poem: Þat kann ek annat, literally 'that I know as a second thing', with þat as the object and the ordinal standing in apposition to it — annat, it þriðia, it fiórða, it fimta, and so on. It is worth reading once and then not again; from here the formula simply marks the count. The Codex Regius does not write annat at all but the numeral ıı, and Neckel's apparatus adds that it does the same in the stanzas that follow, which is why the printed text shows 'it þriðia' and the rest where the manuscript has figures. Three lines and no content: we are told who needs the charm and nothing about what it is or does. læknar is a nominative plural standing predicatively with lifa — to live as healers, to live by healing — and the withholding is the poem's design, not damage to the text.

sentences.t:
Þat kann ek it þriðia:
ef mér verðr þǫrf mikil
hapts við mína heiptmǫgo,
eggiar ek deyfi
minna andskota,
bítat þeim vápn né vélir.
sentences.l:
That I know as the third:
if great need comes upon me
of a fetter against my foes,
I blunt the edges
of my adversaries,
weapons bite not for them, nor wiles.
sentences.i: I know a third: if I have great need of a fetter for my enemies, I blunt my adversaries' blades — then their weapons bite no more, and their contrivances do not either.
sentences.n: The third charm. verðr mér þǫrf is impersonal, 'need becomes to me', with hapts a genitive after þǫrf: the need is of a hapt, a bond or fetter, and the word returns as a literal fetter in the next stanza. heiptmǫgr is one of the poem's compact hate-words — heipt 'feud, hatred' plus mǫgr 'son, man' — a man bound to you by enmity as others are bound by kin. Then the effect, and only the effect: eggiar ek deyfi, 'I blunt the edges'. The last line has to be construed with care, because the obvious English gets it backwards. bítat is bíta with the suffixed negative, and its subject is the plural vápn né vélir; þeim is DATIVE, and bíta takes the accusative, so þeim cannot be what is bitten. It is a dative of disadvantage and possession, resuming minna andskota of the line before: the weapons and wiles that fail are the foes' own. 'Weapons bite not for them' — a blunted edge does not bite, and the blunted edges are theirs. Read the other way the charm would make the speaker's enemies invulnerable, which is the reverse of what lines 4–5 have just set up. vél is a wile or contrivance — also, concretely, an engine or device, which is what makes bíta apt of it alongside vápn — and pairing it with weapons says the charm stops the cunning attack as well as the direct one. Neckel prints it in line 1 although his apparatus records that the Codex Regius omits it here while writing it in the following stanzas; the word is set in roman, not italic, so we transcribe it plain. Sijmons rewrites line 6 as bítat vápn heldr en velir? after a passage in Heimskringla; the apparatus prints velir without the acute Neckel's own text gives it. Nothing is said about how the fetter is laid on, or what is said, or when.

sentences.t:
Þat kann ek it fiórða:
ef mér fyrðar bera
bǫnd at boglimom,
svá ek gel,
at ek ganga má;
sprettr mér af fótom fiǫturr,
en af hǫndom hapt.
sentences.l:
That I know as the fourth:
if men bear against me
bonds at my arms,
so I chant
that I can walk;
the fetter springs from my feet,
and from my hands the bond.
sentences.i: I know a fourth: if men put bonds on my arms, I chant so that I can walk free — the fetter springs off my feet, and the shackle off my hands.
sentences.n: The fourth charm, and the one described most fully, which is to say in two clauses. gel is gala, 'to crow, to chant' — the verb behind galdr, the ordinary word for a spell — and it is the only place in these five stanzas where the poem says what the charm physically is: something sung. svá … at with the indicative má gives the result, 'so I chant that I can walk' — a statement of fact, not a wish, which is why the literal layer avoids 'may'. mér in line 2 is a dative of disadvantage, doing the work of a possessive with boglimom: the bonds are borne against me, onto my arms. Watch bǫnd: the shared glossary carries bǫndom from st. 109 as a poetic name for the gods, but here the word is the plain plural of band and the bonds are ropes. boglimom is bógr 'shoulder' plus limr 'limb', so the bonds are on the arms; Neckel prints it without the acute, where the Codex Regius and Rask have bóglimom. The last two lines put fiǫtr and hapt in parallel, feet and hands, and spretta is 'to spring, to start off' — the fetter comes away of itself rather than being undone. There is no fettering scene anywhere in the poem to attach this to.

sentences.t:
Þat kann ek it fimta:
ef ek sé af fári skotinn
flein í fólk vaða,
flýgra hann svá stint,
at ek stǫðvigak,
ef ek hann siónom of sék.
sentences.l:
That I know as the fifth:
if I see, shot out of malice,
a shaft wade into the host,
it flies not so hard
that I do not stop it,
if I see it with my eyes.
sentences.i: I know a fifth: if I see a shaft shot in malice driving into the host, it never flies so hard that I cannot stop it — as long as I catch sight of it.
sentences.n: The fifth charm, and here the poem does say what the operative condition is: sight. Everything hangs on the last line, and of sék is siá with the old expletive of and the enclitic pronoun -k fused on, 'I see it'. The negatives are the difficulty. Old Norse puts one in each clause — flýgra is fliúga with the suffixed -a, and stǫðvigak carries the first person twice over: stǫðvi (the subjunctive) + -g- (the enclitic ek, voiced between vowels, exactly as in kennig at 163,2) + -a (the negative) + -k (the enclitic ek again). With the free ek standing before it, 'I' is expressed three times in four syllables. So the sentence reads 'it flies not so hard that I do not stop it'. The literal layer keeps both negatives because that is the shape of the sentence; English idiom wants 'so hard that I cannot stop it', which is what the idiomatic layer says. vaða is 'to wade', used of a missile driving through the air the way a man drives through water — we keep the verb rather than flatten it to 'fly'. af fári is 'out of malice, out of hostility', taking fár as the abstract noun. In line 3 Neckel prints fólk with the k set in italic; the Codex Regius and the editions read the dative fólki, which would give 'wade among the host' rather than 'into' it. The italic marks the ending as Neckel's, not the letter as a supplement — the k stands in the manuscript too. A small difference, and the accusative is Neckel's.

sentences.t:
Þat kann ek it sétta:
ef mik særir þegn
á rótom rás viðar,
ok þann hal,
er mik heipta kveðr,
þann eta mein heldr en mik.
sentences.l:
That I know as the sixth:
if a man wounds me
on the roots of the running tree,
and that man,
who calls hatreds upon me,
him may the harms eat rather than me.
sentences.i: The sixth I know: if a man wounds me at the roots of the running tree, then the man who calls hatreds upon me — let the harms eat him instead of me.
sentences.n: The sixth charm. rás viðar in line 3 is a real crux and we do not pretend otherwise: Neckel prints the two words apart, but rás is not a form the noun rás (f.) 'a running, a course' makes in the genitive (that would be rásar), so the phrase is best taken as a compound rásviðr written open, 'the running tree/wood' — and nobody has explained what a running wood is. No editor has construed the compound securely, and Neckel prints the two words apart without comment. We render the words and flag them rather than choose; 'running tree' in both layers is a placeholder, not a construal. What the charm is for is clearer than its wording: harm worked on a man at a tree's roots, turned back on the one who worked it. kveðia here takes an accusative of the person and a genitive of the thing he is called upon for — heipta, the genitive plural of heipt 'hatred, feud, curse'. mein is a nominative plural and the subject: the harms do the eating, and eta stands in the plain present with no subjunctive marking, so the wish is carried by the sentence rather than by the mood. Neckel's apparatus records that Finnur Jónsson would delete the ok of line 4.

sentences.t:
Þat kann ek it siaunda:
ef ek sé hávan loga
sal um sessmǫgom,
brennrat svá breitt,
at ek hánom biargigak;
þann kann ek galdr at gala.
sentences.l:
That I know as the seventh:
if I see the high hall blazing
over the bench-companions,
it burns not so broad
that I may not save him;
that charm I know how to chant.
sentences.i: The seventh I know: if I see the high hall blazing over the men on the benches, it never burns so wide that I cannot bring him out. That is a charm I know how to chant.
sentences.n: The seventh charm, and the line Neckel prints — ef ek sé hávan loga / sal um sessmǫgom — is contested on grammatical grounds. hávan is a strong accusative singular masculine and agrees exactly with sal, which makes loga the infinitive of loga 'to blaze' in an accusative-and-infinitive after sé: I see the high hall blazing. The alternative reads hávan loga as 'a high flame', accusative of the weak noun logi, and then sal has no word to govern it. The editors were uneasy: Neckel prints the manuscript's hávan and records three conjectures against the line — Hildebrand's hátt um, Bugge's sofandom, Gering's sviðinn — the first two with a question mark. Both clauses of lines 4–5 carry a negative and both are meant: brennrat … at ek … biargigak is 'it does not burn so wide that I cannot save him', i.e. no fire is ever wide enough to keep me from bringing him out. English carries the same double negative. brennrat is brennr with the suffixed -at, and biargigak packs four things into one word: the subjunctive biargi, the enclitic pronoun (written -g), the negative -a, and the enclitic pronoun again as -k. hánom is singular where sessmǫgom was plural, and it is not decidable whether the man or the hall is what gets saved; the poem supplies no possessive for sessmǫgom, so neither do we.

sentences.t:
Þat kann ek it átta,
er ǫllom er
nytsamlikt at nema:
hvars hatr vex
með hildings sonom,
þat má ek bœta brátt.
sentences.l:
That I know as the eighth,
which for all is
useful to take up:
wherever hatred grows
among a prince's sons,
that I can amend quickly.
sentences.i: The eighth I know, and it is a useful thing for anyone to take up: wherever hatred springs up among a chieftain's sons, I can mend it, and quickly.
sentences.n: The eighth charm — the one item in the list recommended to the audience rather than kept back: ǫllom … nytsamlikt at nema, useful for everyone to take up. nema is the poem's own verb for taking in what is offered, the same verb as the Loddfáfnir refrain's ef þú nemr and as st. 164's sá er nam, and quite distinct from the conjunction nema 'unless' that opens 163,7. hildingr is a poetic word for a war-leader, so hildings synir are the sons of a chief, and the charm is aimed at feud inside a ruling house. hvars is the contracted hvar es 'wherever'. No apparatus entry.

sentences.t:
Þat kann ek it níunda:
ef mik nauðr um stendr,
at biarga fari míno á floti,
vind ek kyrri
vági á
ok svæfik allan sæ.
sentences.l:
That I know as the ninth:
if need presses upon me,
to save my ship afloat,
the wind I still
upon the wave
and I put all the sea to sleep.
sentences.i: The ninth I know: if I am hard pressed to save my ship out on the water, I still the wind on the wave and lull the whole sea to sleep.
sentences.n: The ninth charm. nauðr is the nominative subject and mik the accusative object of standa — need besets the man — with um the old expletive particle the poem sets before verbs (compare sér um getr, st. 8,2). far is any vessel, and fari is the dative that biarga governs, the same construction as 152's hánom biargigak. The last two lines are one gesture split at the caesura: kyrra 'to still' and svæfa 'to lull asleep' are both causatives, the second built straight on sofa 'to sleep', so the sea is not merely quieted but put to sleep; svæfik is svæfi ek with the enclitic pronoun. No apparatus entry.

sentences.t:
Þat kann ek it tíunda:
ef ek sé túnriðor
leika lopti á,
ek svá vinnk,
at þær villar fara
sinna heim hama,
sinna heim huga.
sentences.l:
That I know as the tenth:
if I see fence-riders
playing in the air,
I so work it
that they fare astray
of their own home-shapes,
of their own home-minds.
sentences.i: The tenth I know: if I see fence-riders at play up in the air, I work it so that they go astray of their own home-shapes and their own home-minds.
sentences.n: The tenth charm. túnriða is a 'home-field rider' — tún is the enclosed ground round a farm — one of the old words for a woman who rides out at night in another shape; we render it fence-rider throughout. leika lopti á is what they are seen doing, an accusative-and-infinitive after sé like the one at st. 152. vinnk is vinn ek. The last two lines are the hardest in the stanza, and the apparatus shows how the editors divided over them: the Codex Regius writes heim hama and heim huga as two words each, and Neckel prints them so; the Copenhagen edition joined them into heimhama, glossing it 'natural shapes', and heimhuga, and the Corpus poeticum boreale read heimhaga 'home pastures'. Whichever way the words are joined, sinna is the genitive plural of the reflexive possessive and hama and huga are genitives too, governed by villar — Old Norse goes astray *of* a thing. The charm strands the riders outside what is theirs: the shape they left behind and the mind that belongs with it. The apparatus also records that R abbreviates þær and reads villir where Neckel, following Lüning, prints villar; Neckel marks the editorial letter by italicizing the a, which the house rule sets plain.

sentences.t:
Þat kann ek it ellipta:
ef ek skal til orrosto
leiða langvini,
und randir ek gel,
en þeir með ríki fara
heilir hildar til,
heilir hildi frá,
koma þeir heilir hvaðan.
sentences.l:
That I know as the eleventh:
if I must to battle
lead long-time friends,
under the shield-rims I chant,
and they fare with power
whole to the battle,
whole from the battle,
they come whole from wherever.
sentences.i: The eleventh I know: if I have to lead old friends into a fight, I chant under the shield-rims, and they go in strength — unhurt to the battle, unhurt from it, and back unhurt from wherever they have been.
sentences.n: The eleventh charm. langvinir are 'long-friends', men held by long acquaintance, and the compound is one of the poem's quiet ones. und takes the accusative in und randir, motion under the raised shields rather than rest beneath them. rǫnd is the rim of a shield and by extension the shield itself. The close turns on one word repeated three times with the preposition swapped around it: heilir, nominative plural of heill 'whole, unhurt', with hildar til taking the genitive and hildi frá the dative, both postposed after their nouns as this metre likes. The same adjective comes back as the greeting Heill! in the last stanza of the poem. til orrosto in line 2 is a genitive, not the dative of st. 129. Eight lines. No apparatus entry.

sentences.t:
Þat kann ek it tólpta:
ef ek sé á tré uppi
váfa virgilná,
sva ek ríst
ok í rúnom fák,
at sá gengr gumi
ok mælir við mik.
sentences.l:
That I know as the twelfth:
if I see up in a tree
a halter-corpse swinging,
so I carve
and in runes I colour
that that man walks
and speaks with me.
sentences.i: The twelfth I know: if I see a hanged man swinging up in a tree, I carve and I paint the runes in such a way that the man walks and speaks with me.
sentences.n: The twelfth charm, and the one that goes with Óðinn's by-name Hangaguð, god of the hanged (Cleasby–Vigfússon s.v. hangi); compare his own hanging at st. 138. virgilnár is a corpse on the virgill, the rope or halter; váfa 'to dangle, to swing' is another infinitive after sé. Line 5's fák is fá ek, from fá 'to draw, to paint, to colour in' — the technical verb for filling a cut rune with pigment or blood. The pair rísta ok fá, cut and colour, is the whole operation, and it is the pair the Rúnatal asks about: veitstu, hvé rísta skal? veitstu, hvé fá skal? (st. 144). sá gengr gumi keeps its demonstrative: that man, the one on the rope. The result clause is indicative, gengr and mælir, not subjunctive: the outcome is stated as fact. Neckel prints sva here without the acute, though svá at 152,4, 155,4 and 159,6. No apparatus entry.

sentences.t:
Þat kann ek it þrettánda:
ef ek skal þegn ungan
verpa vatni á,
munat hann falla,
þótt hann í fólk komi,
hnígra sá halr fyr hiǫrom.
sentences.l:
That I know as the thirteenth:
if I must cast water
upon a young man,
he will not fall,
though he come into the host,
that man will not sink before swords.
sentences.i: The thirteenth I know: if I have to pour water over a young man, he will not fall — he can go into the host and not go down before the swords.
sentences.n: The thirteenth charm, and the one piece of household ritual in the list. verpa vatni á is the water-pouring the sagas describe at the naming of a child (ausa vatni), and is generally taken to be older than Christian baptism; the poem's þegn ungan is a young man rather than an infant, which sits awkwardly with that. þegn is a free man, here ungan, still young. Both verbs in the second half carry the suffixed negative the charms favour: munat is mun + -at, hnígra is hnígr + -a. fólk in verse is not 'the people' but the armed host and by extension the battle, and hiǫrom 'swords' in the last line keeps it there. No apparatus entry.

sentences.t:
Þat kann ek it fiórtánda:
ef ek skal fyrða liði
telia tíva fyrir,
ása ok álfa
ek kann allra skil;
fár kann ósnotr svá.
sentences.i: The fourteenth I know: if I have to count the gods over before a company of men, I know the marks of every one of them, Æsir and elves alike. Few who lack wisdom know as much.
sentences.n: The fourteenth charm, and the boast is plain scholarship: to name and tell apart every god on demand. kunna skil e-s is the idiom, 'to know the distinctions of', and allra is the genitive plural gathering ása ok álfa under it — those two are the genitives in the stanza. tíva is not: it is the accusative object of telia, and the accusative and genitive plural of this word happen to be alike. fyrða liði is a dative, 'for a host of men', and the fyrir at the end of line 3 is the preposition governing it, postposed as prepositions regularly are here — telia fyrir e-m, 'to count over before someone'. The last line has fár as a masculine singular agreeing with ósnotr — 'few an unwise man knows so' — a collective singular English has to spread out; and this fár is the adjective 'few', not the noun fár 'harm, malice' glossed earlier in the poem. No apparatus entry.

sentences.t:
Þat kann ek it fimtánda,
er gól Þióðrørir,
dvergr, fyr Dellings durom:
afl gól hann ásom,
en álfom frama,
hyggio Hroptatý.
sentences.l:
That I know as the fifteenth,
which Þióðrørir chanted,
the dwarf, before Dellingr's doors:
strength he chanted to the Æsir,
and advancement to the elves,
understanding to Hroptatýr.
sentences.i: The fifteenth I know, the one Þióðrørir the dwarf chanted before Dellingr's doors: he chanted strength to the Æsir, advancement to the elves, and understanding to Hroptatýr.
sentences.n: The fifteenth charm, and the only one in the list whose chanter is named — and he is someone other than the speaker, so the charm is quoted, known at second hand. Þióðrørir is attested only here (Cleasby–Vigfússon cites no other line); the Codex Regius writes the name as two words, Þióð reyrir, and Neckel's Þióðrørir is his normalization of that. Dellingr is the father of Day at Vafþrúðnismál 25, so fyr Dellings durom is usually taken to mean at daybreak. gala takes the dative of whoever the chant is for — ásom, álfom, Hroptatý — and Hroptatýr is one of Óðinn's own names, which is what makes the last line turn strange: the chant that gave the gods strength and the elves advancement gave Óðinn thought. Þióðrørir is printed with a thorn, Dellings with a true D — the only word in these stanzas that opens with a genuine capital D.

sentences.t:
Þat kann ek it sextánda:
ef ek vil ins svinna mans
hafa geð allt ok gaman,
hugi ek hverfi
hvítarmri kono
ok sný ek hennar ǫllom sefa.
sentences.l:
That I know as the sixteenth:
if I want of the clever girl
to have all the mind and the delight,
the thoughts I turn
of the white-armed woman
and I turn all her feeling.
sentences.i: The sixteenth I know: if I want the whole mind of a clever girl, and her pleasure too, I turn the thoughts of the white-armed woman, and turn all her feeling.
sentences.n: The sixteenth charm, and it belongs with the Billingr story of st. 96–102 rather than with the battle charms: this is the seduction that works, told by the speaker whom a woman once left a dog in her place for. svinnr is the wise man's adjective of the gnomic stanzas (sviðr, st. 103), and here it is on man, the young woman — the poem's habit of praising a woman's intelligence just before overriding it holds to the end. Two verbs of turning, and they take different cases: hverfi is the weak causative hverfa 'to turn something', with hugi as its accusative plural object and hvítarmri kono as the dative of the person whose thoughts they are — distinct from the strong intransitive hverfa of st. 99's hvarf ek 'I turned away'; snúa then governs its object in the dative outright, ǫllom sefa. hvítarmr 'white-armed' is a standing epithet of the older poetry. No apparatus entry.

sentences.t:
Þat kann ek it siautiánda,
at mik mun seint firraz
it manunga man; —
lióða þessa
munðu, Loddfáfnir,
lengi vanr vera;
þó sé þér góð, ef þú getr,
nýt, ef þú nemr,
þǫrf, ef þú þiggr.
sentences.l:
That I know as the seventeenth,
that slow to shun me will be
the youthful girl; —
of these songs
you will, Loddfáfnir,
long be wanting;
yet may they be good for you, if you get them,
useful, if you take them,
needful, if you receive them.
sentences.i: The seventeenth I know: the young girl will be slow to turn away from me. — These songs, Loddfáfnir, you will long go without; and yet, may they do you good if you come by them, serve you if you take them in, help you if you accept them.
sentences.n: The seventeenth charm, and the stanza breaks in half at Neckel's em-dash. Lines 1–3 are the charm and are one clause, with the subject held to the last line as this poem likes: firraz is the middle voice of firra 'to remove', so 'to take oneself away from', and mik is its accusative. Then the poem turns and speaks to Loddfáfnir — the only time his name appears outside the counsels of st. 111–137, and the plainest sign that the Ljóðatal has been stitched to the rest of the poem. munðu is munt þú, the auxiliary with the enclitic pronoun; Neckel prints it with ð, and the same letters would spell the imperative of muna 'to remember', but vanr vera in line 6 needs the auxiliary. vanr with the genitive lióða þessa is 'lacking' these songs, not 'accustomed to' them: Old Norse has both adjectives and the case decides, genitive for want and dative for habit. So the charms are withheld from the very man the poem spent twenty-seven stanzas instructing. Lines 7–9 take up the two-line promise of the Loddfáfnir refrain — nióta mundo, ef þú nemr, / þér muno góð, ef þú getr — and open it into three, adding þǫrf, ef þú þiggr to góð and nýt; þǫrf in line 9 is not the noun 'need' but the neuter plural of the adjective þarfr, and the plural all three agree with is the lióð of line 4. The editors felt the seams here: Neckel records that Bugge assumed three lost lines between lines 1 and 2, that Hildebrand assumed a gap after line 3, that Hildebrand would read þótt for þó in line 7, and that Gering rewrote that line entire as þótt þér góð séi, ef geta mættir. Nine lines.

sentences.t:
Þat kann ek it áttiánda,
er ek æva kennig
mey né mannz kono —
allt er betra,
er einn um kann;
þat fylgir lióða lokom —,
nema þeiri einni,
er mik armi verr
eða min systir sé.
sentences.l:
That I know as the eighteenth,
which I never teach
to maiden nor to man's wife —
all is better,
which one alone knows;
that follows at the songs' close —,
except to her alone
who wraps me in her arm
or is my sister.
sentences.i: The eighteenth I know, and it is the one I never teach to any girl or to any man's wife — everything is better that one man knows alone; that is what comes at the ending of the songs — except for one woman only, the one whose arm is around me, or else my own sister.
sentences.n: The eighteenth charm, and Óðinn will not say what it is. The refusal is the whole content: er ek æva kennig, 'which I never teach', with kennig for kenni ek. The grammar of the two people withheld from is not tidy. kono is either accusative or dative, since kona makes the same form for both, but mey is an accusative where kenna would ordinarily want a dative of the person taught, and þeiri einni in line 7 is unambiguously dative. Neckel prints what the manuscript has and the inconsistency stands. Lines 4–6, inside the dashes, are an aside in the gnomic voice of the Gestaþáttr — allt er betra, er einn um kann, everything is better that one knows alone — followed by þat fylgir lióða lokom, 'that goes with the ending of the songs', which reads like a remark about the poem written into the poem. Then the exception, and it is narrow: armi is the dative of armr 'arm', and verr here is the third singular of veria 'to wrap, to enclose', not the comparative adverb verr 'worse' that the poem has used before — the woman whose arm is around him, or his sister. nema in line 7 is the conjunction 'except', not the verb nema 'to take in' of st. 153,3. Neckel prints min without the acute here, beside míno at 154,3. Nine lines, and no apparatus entry at all: for the most withheld stanza in the poem the editors had nothing to propose.

sentences.t:
Nú ero Háva mál kveðin,
Háva hǫllo í,
allþǫrf ýta sonom,
óþǫrf iǫtna sonom.
Heill, sá er kvað!
Heill, sá er kann!
Nióti, sá er nam!
Heilir, þeirs hlýddo!
sentences.l:
Now the High One's sayings have been spoken,
in the High One's hall,
all-needful to the sons of men,
un-needful to the sons of giants.
Hail, he who spoke!
Hail, he who knows!
May he have the use of it, who took it in!
Hail, they who listened!
sentences.i: Now the High One's sayings have been recited, in the High One's own hall — needful through and through for the sons of men, of no use at all to the sons of giants. Hail to the man who spoke them, hail to the man who knows them; may the man who took them in have the good of them; and hail to everyone who listened.
sentences.n: The end of the poem. It names itself in its own last stanza — Háva mál, the sayings of the High One, a neuter plural — and hands the naming over to whoever is reciting: mál is the nominative plural subject of ero, and kveðin is a past participle agreeing with it, 'have been spoken', with no speaker claimed. allþǫrf and óþǫrf are nominative plural neuters agreeing with mál too and are built as a matched pair, all- 'wholly' against ó- 'un-', so the same sayings are entirely needful and entirely useless depending on who is listening; they are the adjective þarfr, the same word that closed st. 162. The last four lines are the formula a reciter speaks at the finish, each a nominative used as an exclamation: heill 'hale, whole' as a greeting — the adjective that meant bodily unhurt at st. 156 — and nióti, third singular subjunctive of nióta. kvað, kann and nióti are all left without an object in the Norse; English cannot leave them so, and we supply one. þeirs is þeir es, 'those who'. Neckel's apparatus records three things here. R reads ýta in line 4, repeating line 3, and iǫtna is a correction written in the margin by a younger hand, which is why Neckel sets it in italic — the fine antithesis of men against giants may be somebody's later improvement. Müllenhoff would delete the Háva of line 2, the second of the two in the stanza; Gering would read hlýddo á. And Neckel's last cross-reference, s. zu 137, sends the reader back to the apparatus of st. 137, where he notes that Müllenhoff moved this closing stanza up to follow the Loddfáfnir counsels and that the paper manuscripts head st. 138 ff. as a separate Rúnatals þáttr Óðins. So the poem's editors could not agree on where it ends, and the manuscript's own ending is the one printed here: four blessings, and no summary of anything that was said.
